claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, and 6, build a paired activation dataset using publicly available HarmBench and JailbreakBench harmful requests, their jailbreak templates, and benign controls from WildGuardMix. Run at least two open-weight safety-aligned models, such as Llama-2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-Instruct, retaining only harmful requests for which the direct prompt is refused and at least one jailbreak version is judged compliant by both the HarmBench evaluator and blinded human review. Add benign prompts wrapped in the same jailbreak templates to control for template recognition. Record every attention-head output and residual-stream state at the final instruction token and during the first generated tokens. Train diagnostic linear probes only on direct harmful versus matched benign prompts, then freeze them and test whether harmfulness remains decodable from successful jailbreak activations, both globally and from individual heads not implicated in refusal. Compare probe AUROC and cross-validated representational similarity between direct and jailbroken versions, controlling for token position, prompt length, and jailbreak family. Persistent, cross-attack decodability—especially from many non-refusal heads—would reject elimination and support bypass; a collapse to chance across layers and heads would support elimination, while persistence only for particular attacks or models would narrow the claim. This diagnostic probe is evidence about representation rather than the claimed training-free detector. The experiment could be skipped if public activation traces and frozen-probe results already cover paired successful jailbreaks, template-matched benign controls, multiple models, and held-out attack families.

To address subclaims 4 and 5, use the successful paired cases from Experiment 1 to test whether a small, causally sufficient set of attention heads is selectively suppressed. On a discovery split, quantify suppression as the reduction under jailbreaks in each head’s refusal-direction contribution and output magnitude relative to the corresponding direct harmful prompt and template-matched benign controls. Identify the smallest head set whose clean-to-jailbreak path patching has a large mediated effect, then freeze that set before testing. On held-out requests and attack families, perform reciprocal interventions: restore those heads’ direct-prompt activations during a jailbreak and, more critically, scale those heads in an otherwise unchanged direct harmful prompt down to their observed jailbreak levels. Measure refusal rate, harmful-compliance rate, and generated-content severity, and compare against equal-sized random heads, magnitude-matched heads, whole-layer interventions, and interventions on proposed continuation heads. If suppressing only the frozen small set reliably converts direct refusals to harmful compliance, while restoring it reverses jailbreaks, the result supports selective suppression and causal sufficiency; restoration without refusal-to-compliance sufficiency would indicate that the heads are necessary mediators but not sufficient, and effects requiring many heads or varying completely by attack/model would refute the strong sparse-subset claim. Existing evidence would make this unnecessary only if it released reproducible reciprocal interventions—not merely ablations—on held-out prompts, attacks, and models with matched-head controls.

To address subclaims 7, 8, and 9, preregister a genuinely training-free harmful-input readout from the persistent heads identified earlier and evaluate it on held-out HarmBench, JailbreakBench, and WildGuardMix examples, including successful jailbreaks, ordinary harmful prompts, benign prompts, and benign prompts using adversarial wrappers. For a strict zero-training test, apply the model’s existing final normalization and unembedding to each selected head’s residual contribution and compute a fixed contrast between preregistered unsafe/refusal tokens and safe/compliance tokens; aggregate heads using a fixed mean or maximum, with no learned weights, probe fitting, or threshold tuning. Report threshold-free AUROC and AUPRC plus TPR at fixed FPRs; separately label any variant using a calibration split as calibration-only rather than training-free. Compare identical test examples against publicly available dedicated moderators such as Llama Guard 3, ShieldGemma, and WildGuard, with bootstrap confidence intervals and stratification by model, attack family, and whether the jailbreak succeeded. Competitive performance under the strict readout would support direct detection without additional training; performance competitive only after fitting a probe or selecting weights would refute the no-additional-training portion, while poor transfer to unseen attacks would show that persistence does not imply a useful detector. This experiment could be omitted if a public benchmark already provides the exact frozen readout specification, untouched test sets, predictions from the dedicated safety models, and auditable confirmation that no detector parameters or thresholds were fitted on evaluation-related data.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct within-request comparison of safety-relevant internal activation under a successful attack and under the corresponding refusal, spanning layers and component types, so persistence can be distinguished from global erasure.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 constructs matched refused/direct and successful-jailbreak cases, records head and residual activations across layers and generation positions, and tests whether harmfulness remains decodable in the successful condition. Its frozen diagnostic probes and direct-versus-jailbroken representational comparison provide an alternative way to establish persistence rather than requiring the particular refusal-direction measurement.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A paired collection of identical harmful requests in refused and successful-jailbreak conditions, with varied attack conditions and clean controls, allowing attack effects to be separated from differences in the underlying requests.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 explicitly retains harmful requests whose direct versions are refused and whose jailbreak versions are compliant, while adding template-matched benign controls and multiple attack families. This supplies the paired successful cases needed for the downstream analyses; the particular source collections and exact yield are not binding requirements of the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A component-level procedure that quantifies which heads are selectively reduced, distinguishes the reduced subset from other heads, and provides a defensible way to freeze and validate that classification.
reference_coverage.rationale: The paired activations from proposed experiment 0 feed proposed experiment 1's head-level measurement of refusal-direction contribution and output suppression. The smallest set is selected on a discovery split, frozen, and tested with held-out requests and attack families against matched random, magnitude-matched, whole-layer, and continuation-head controls. This supplies the same discriminating knowledge through causal/path-patching selection rather than the reference's particular overlap statistic and cutoff sweep.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled causal intervention showing whether reducing only the candidate head subset converts a normally refusing harmful input into compliance, with equal-sized noncandidate interventions and uncertainty estimates to exclude generic perturbation effects.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 scales the candidate heads in an otherwise direct harmful prompt down to their observed jailbreak levels and measures refusal, harmful compliance, and severity. It includes held-out cases and several matched controls, including equal-sized random heads, and also tests restoration in the reverse direction. This directly tests causal sufficiency and is at least as discriminating as the reference intervention.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that heads outside the selectively suppressed subset still carry harmful-content information during successful jailbreaks, ideally with a comparison to the corresponding direct harmful condition.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 tests harmfulness decodability from individual heads not implicated in refusal as well as globally, specifically on successful jailbreak activations and matched direct prompts. Proposed experiment 1 additionally distinguishes those heads from the candidate suppressed set through reciprocal and continuation-head interventions. A direct readout of retained harmful information establishes the stated persistence without requiring the reference's exact mean-absolute-activation calculation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A discrimination between attack-template-specific head specialization and the rival explanation that the candidate head types merely differ in their intrinsic sensitivity to harmful content, by isolating responses to the harmful request from responses to the attack template.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed paired direct-versus-jailbreak comparisons and template-matched benign controls address the same confound at the whole-prompt level, and the per-head suppression measurements can reveal attack-associated changes. However, the set does not explicitly decompose each head's activation into original harmful-request-token and attack-template-token contributions or establish the two types' equality on harmful content and separation on template content. The proposed outcomes could therefore leave a difference in intrinsic harmful-content sensitivity or harmful-content/template interaction as an alternative explanation.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment distinguishes the mechanistic account from a rival explanation by separately attributing each head's response to harmful-request tokens and attack-template tokens.
The proposed experiments keep the harmful request paired and add template-matched benign controls, which tests persistence and reduces—but does not isolate—the two sources of activation.

Their interventions and probes operate on whole prompt/head representations and do not report the type-wise token-source decomposition required to show equal harmful-token responses and divergent template-token responses.
Consequently, a discovered difference between the head types could still be due to head-specific harmful-content sensitivity or an unresolved interaction between harmful content and template context.
A team running the proposed set would fail to learn decisively whether the proposed specialization mechanism defeats that rival explanation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An externally evaluated, training-free harmful-input readout that transfers across held-out safety tasks and multiple safety-aligned models and is quantitatively compared with dedicated safety systems.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 specifies a fixed, zero-training readout using selected persistent-head contributions, evaluates held-out harmful, benign, wrapped, and successful-jailbreak examples across several benchmark conditions, and reports threshold-free and fixed-operating-point metrics. It compares the same examples with dedicated moderators and stratifies results by model and attack family. The number and identity of benchmarks or models used in the reference are not binding, and the proposal directly tests both the no-additional-training and competitive-quality parts of the claim.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly tests persistence versus erasure, constructs matched successful jailbreak pairs, identifies and causally manipulates a sparse head subset, tests representation in other heads, and evaluates a genuinely training-free detector against dedicated safety systems. The remaining gap is mechanistic rather than a missing core claim test: without separating harmful-request-token contributions from attack-template-token contributions, favorable results would not fully rule out the stated rival explanation for why the head types differ.

Reference experiment 5 would add a stronger token-level explanation of why the head types differ, but that rival-explanation decomposition is not itself stated in the claim and the proposed matched controls plus causal interventions still test every listed subclaim. The proposed outcomes would therefore settle the claim, while leaving that finer mechanistic attribution less directly established.
